page.text:
A fundamental way to compare two mathematical sets is through the relation
of *inclusion* or *subsethood*. We say that a set $A$ is a subset of $B$,
denoted $A \subseteq B$, when every element belonging to $A$ also belongs
to $B$.

It is essential to distinguish between the primitive relation of
membership ($x \in A$) and the derivative relation of inclusion ($A
\subseteq B$). Membership relates an individual entity to an enclosing
collection and is non-transitive: $x \in y$ and $y \in z$ do not imply $x
\in z$. Inclusion, by contrast, is a relationship between sets defined
universally: it is reflexive ($A \subseteq A$) and transitive ($A
\subseteq B$ and $B \subseteq C$ imply $A \subseteq C$).
